section_summary: This section assembles intelligence and diplomatic reporting on Japanese troop dispositions and movements from October 1940 through December 1941. It covers garrisons across China and Manchuria, withdrawals and embarkations from Canton, Shanghai, Haiphong, Kobe, and Woosung, reported concentrations for operations against Singapore or Southeast Asia, and large troop landings at Dairen. The section also contains statistical naval-intelligence reports, cross-reference sheets, internal paraphrases, and conversations with British and Chinese diplomats assessing Japanese intentions.

subfiles.title: Confidential List of Present Japanese Division Locations
subfiles.to: United States military, naval, and executive officials
subfiles.about: Lists the believed current stations of Japanese divisions and the Imperial Guard.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum provides a division-by-division inventory of Japanese military locations in Japan, Korea, Manchuria, and occupied China. Stations include Tokyo, Qiqihar, Harbin, Yichang, Hailar, Canton, Tianjin, Taiwan, and numerous provincial fronts. The final page is principally a distribution list for senior American departments and intelligence offices.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Japanese Forces and Concessions in French Indochina
subfiles.about: References a telegram on Japanese concessions, a Hainan concentration, and withdrawals from Guangxi.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Saigon telegram No. 31 concerning Japanese military concessions in French Indochina. It notes reports of a large concentration at Hainan, an almost complete withdrawal from Guangxi, and speculation about Japanese intentions in Indochina.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Japanese Troops in Dairen
subfiles.about: References a message quoting the American consul at Dairen on Japanese troops there.
subfiles.summary: The filing note points to a January 29 telegram from Japan. That telegram quoted a January 28 message from the American consul at Dairen concerning Japanese troops.

subfiles.title: Hanoi Telegram No. 46 on Troops Embarking at Haiphong
subfiles.about: Reports the departure of about 3,500 jungle-trained Japanese soldiers from Haiphong.
subfiles.summary: Reliable reports said approximately 3,500 Japanese soldiers had embarked at Haiphong for an unknown destination. They had received special jungle training near Lang Son, including maneuver and trail-opening work. Observers speculated that they might be used in Thailand against adjoining British territory or the Burma Road.

subfiles.title: Hanoi Telegram No. 48 on Withdrawals from Tonkin and Saigon
subfiles.about: Reports withdrawals of Japanese troops and modern artillery from northern and southern Indochina.
subfiles.summary: The sender estimated that about 5,000 Japanese soldiers had been withdrawn from Tonkin. The chief of the Military Cabinet expected all Japanese military personnel to leave Saigon shortly. Modern artillery was reportedly being shipped away from Haiphong and replaced by older guns, although additional light tanks had recently arrived.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Reports on Japanese Naval and Troop Movements
subfiles.about: References instructions to continue telegraphic reporting on Japanese naval vessels and troop movements.
subfiles.summary: The filing material refers to Saigon telegram No. 19. Its subject is the movement of Japanese naval vessels and troops, and it records an instruction that telegraphic reports on those movements should continue.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 546 on a Reported Plan to Attack Singapore
subfiles.about: Relays reports that twelve to fifteen Japanese divisions were concentrated for an imminent attack on Singapore.
subfiles.summary: Two sources, an American correspondent and a foreign diplomat, reported concentrations in Kyushu, Taiwan, and Hainan intended for an assault on Singapore. The attack was supposedly to occur within days and perhaps coincide with a German attack on the Suez Canal. The correspondent identified retired General Ishihara as a source who said the move had been decided upon but that he opposed it.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 546
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the reported Japanese plan for an imminent attack on Singapore.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase repeats the claim that twelve or thirteen Japanese divisions were concentrated in Kyushu, Taiwan, and Hainan. It connects the projected Singapore attack with German action against the Suez Canal and identifies General Ishihara as a reported source. Ishihara was said to oppose the decision.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 547 Evaluating the Singapore Report
subfiles.about: Reports the limited results of efforts to assess the credibility of the alleged Singapore plan.
subfiles.summary: The embassy sought information that could help evaluate the previous day's report of an impending Japanese attack. Its only confirmed finding was that the foreign diplomat's own informant was a German businessman.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 547
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the embassy's effort to assess the source behind the Singapore-attack report.
subfiles.summary: The document restates that the embassy was seeking evidence with which to judge telegram No. 546. The sole additional fact obtained was that a German businessman had supplied the information to the diplomat. Page 15 is a poor duplicate copy of the same paraphrase.

subfiles.title: Japanese Troop and Material Movement Through Tientsin in January 1941
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and Department of State
subfiles.about: Tabulates Japanese troops and military matériel passing through Tianjin during January 1941.
subfiles.summary: French sources reported 7,800 troops arriving from the sea toward Beijing and departures toward Tanggu that included troops, wounded men, and dead. Matériel figures included trucks, tanks or armored cars, aircraft, and trains carrying munitions, supplies, and barbed wire. Damaged guns, aircraft, and trucks were among the items shipped out.

subfiles.title: Japanese Troop and Material Movement in North China During 1940
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes a year of Japanese troop and matériel traffic through Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: French military and police sources in Tianjin reported 110,300 Japanese and 17,000 Manchurian arrivals during 1940. Departures included 113,550 Japanese personnel, 40,990 wounded, and 33,500 dead. Incoming equipment included 1,072 trucks, 156 aircraft, 421 tanks or armored cars, and 142 guns.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Chungking Naval-Attaché Report on the Kwangtung Coast
subfiles.about: Describes the reported purpose of Japanese coastal operations in Guangdong and Chinese concern over Matsuoka's diplomacy.
subfiles.summary: Chinese intelligence believed Japanese operations on the Guangdong coast were intended to cut smuggling routes, destroy salt fields, and force Chinese forces inland. Only a few thousand Japanese troops were thought to be involved. Chinese officials were also anxious about Matsuoka's journey to Moscow and Berlin and continuing negotiations with the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Hongkong Station-Ship Report on Coastal Landings
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese landings between Pakhoi and Towshan intended to close smuggling routes.
subfiles.summary: Two regiments from the 38th Division and Second Guards Brigade reportedly made six small landings between Pakhoi and Towshan. Most came from the Canton area rather than Hainan, and their apparent mission was to close smuggling routes after the closure of Bias Bay. The report also recorded heavy transport traffic in the Pearl River and Japanese sales of commercial shipping passes.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation and British Telegram on an Alleged Singapore Plan
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles; British Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.to: Department of State; British Foreign Office
subfiles.about: Records Halifax's delivery of a British report alleging a Japanese plan for a surprise attack on Singapore.
subfiles.summary: Viscount Halifax gave Under Secretary Welles a copy of an April 13 telegram from the British Ambassador at Tokyo. A secret source claimed that twelve to fifteen divisions were assembled in Taiwan and Hainan, with transports ready for a direct attack on Singapore coordinated with German action at Suez. The source believed Japan expected the United States to remain preoccupied with the Atlantic and aid to Britain. The alleged plan avoided preliminary seizure of Indochinese bases so as not to alert Washington.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Shanghai Report on the Occupation of Foochow
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese troops occupied Foochow in Fukien Province.
subfiles.summary: The brief message states that Japanese troops occupied Foochow, Fukien, on the afternoon of April 21. No force strength or operational detail is supplied.

subfiles.title: Canton Telegram No. 35 on Possible Movement to Thailand
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese forces might soon leave Canton for Thailand.
subfiles.summary: A usually reliable source said Japanese forces were to be sent to Thailand and troops at Canton were expected to move soon. The sender suggested that the decision might have contributed to the Japanese cabinet's resignation. Whether the movement occurred was thought to depend on the new cabinet's character and actions.

subfiles.title: Canton Telegram No. 37 on Preparations at Sheklung
subfiles.about: Reports signs that troops at Sheklung and around Canton were preparing to move, possibly to southern Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Japanese troops at Sheklung reportedly ordered the East River closed to craft on July 25 and instructed residents to remain indoors. Reports also described withdrawals from outposts north of Canton and defensive strengthening of other posts. The sender judged that these developments pointed to an early movement of forces from Canton, possibly to southern Indochina.

subfiles.title: Canton Telegram No. 38 on Pearl River Transports
subfiles.about: Reports a decline in empty transports between Bocca Tigris and Whampoa and instability in the military-yen exchange rate.
subfiles.summary: An informant observed fewer empty transports in the Pearl River on July 19 than earlier in the week, although the total remained above normal. Some troops were said to have departed. The Japanese military yen also fell sharply against the Hong Kong dollar before the exchange closed.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1055 Relaying Kobe Transport Movements
subfiles.from: Warner at Kobe, transmitted by Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Reports the departure of about twenty troop and cargo transports from Kobe and Osaka.
subfiles.summary: Approximately twenty Japanese troop and cargo transports left Kobe and Osaka on July 19 and 20, heading through the Inland Sea. Passenger rail travel toward Tokyo was restricted, and foreign access to an arriving ship was denied. The report also mentioned new cargo restrictions favoring Japanese vessels and an armed Italian merchant cruiser in the outer harbor.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Japanese Troop Movement in South China
subfiles.about: References a Hong Kong telegram reporting on Japanese troop movements in South China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Hong Kong telegram No. 264 concerning Japanese troop movements in South China. The original was filed in the State Department's war-related decimal series.

subfiles.title: Canton Telegram No. 39 on Troops Departing for Indochina
subfiles.about: Estimates that about 7,000 Japanese troops had left Canton, probably for Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Further inquiry indicated that roughly half the Japanese troops at Canton, about 7,000 men with equipment and motor trucks, had departed during the preceding ten days. Their destination was presumed to be Indochina, and additional departures were expected. The number of aircraft at the local airfield had also noticeably declined.

subfiles.title: Dairen Telegram Reporting the Arrival of 7,000 Troops
subfiles.to: Tokyo, Mukden, Harbin, Peiping, and the Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports the disembarkation at Dairen of about 7,000 Japanese troops from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Approximately 7,000 Japanese troops, apparently infantry from Japan, had just reached Dairen and were disembarking. The report was marked urgent and circulated widely among American posts in East Asia.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1114 Relaying Heavy Westbound Movement from Kobe
subfiles.from: Warner at Kobe, transmitted by Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Reports unusually heavy westbound troop, freight, and railway traffic.
subfiles.summary: Warner reported from Kobe that westbound troop and freight transports had been exceptionally active during the preceding several days. Railway traffic was likewise very heavy.

subfiles.title: Dairen Telegram on Cavalry and Other Troop Movements
subfiles.to: Tokyo, Mukden, Peiping, and the Department of State
subfiles.about: Clarifies that many of the recently arrived troops at Dairen were cavalry.
subfiles.summary: A considerable portion of the troops reported on July 28 proved to be cavalry. Small bodies of equipped infantry, troops in trucks, and cavalry continued to pass through the city, while further contingents disembarked. Some newly arrived soldiers were reportedly quartered in local schools.

subfiles.title: Dairen Telegram on Increasing Troop Arrivals
subfiles.to: Tokyo, Mukden, Harbin, Peiping, and the Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports continuing landings and an estimate that 40,000 troops had moved north through Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Troop arrivals were continuing on an increasing scale, with multiple transports approaching or reaching Dairen. Soviet sources estimated that approximately 40,000 troops had passed north through the port during the month, many reportedly coming from Central China. A cautiously reported rumor claimed that withdrawals from China had been facilitated by an agreement with Chungking negotiated through Vichy representatives.

subfiles.title: Mukden Telegram No. 42 on Troops Moving Toward the Railway
subfiles.about: Reports several thousand troops, armored cars, and supplies moving toward the railway at Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Although the general military situation was described as materially unchanged, several thousand troops had been observed moving toward the railway. Armored cars and military supplies were also visible, and passenger trains were extraordinarily congested.

subfiles.title: Dairen Telegram on Continuing Cavalry and Infantry Landings
subfiles.to: Tokyo, Mukden, Harbin, Peiping, Chungking, Shanghai, and the Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports that troop landings at Dairen continued to increase and included substantial cavalry forces.
subfiles.summary: At least one quarter of the newly observed troops appeared to be cavalry. The remainder consisted mainly of infantry and motorized supply units. Most or all of the cavalry apparently remained at Dairen.

subfiles.title: Cover Despatch Transmitting Report on Rumored Manchurian Withdrawals
subfiles.from: Kenneth C. Krentz, American Consul at Mukden
subfiles.about: Transmits a copy of a despatch on rumors that Japanese troops were being withdrawn from Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Krentz encloses his confidential despatch to the American Embassy at Peiping concerning alleged Japanese troop withdrawals from Manchuria. The cover letter identifies the enclosure and its distribution to the Department of State.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5: Rumors of Withdrawal of Japanese Troops from Manchuria
subfiles.from: Kenneth C. Krentz, American Consul at Mukden
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Peiping
subfiles.about: Evaluates reports that as many as eight Japanese divisions were leaving Manchuria for China Proper.
subfiles.summary: Radio broadcasts from Shanghai alleged that Japanese troops were moving from Manchuria to China Proper, but the Mukden consulate found no evidence of large-scale changes. The British consular post likewise could not confirm a reported transfer of eight divisions. Krentz cautioned that secret movements through inaccessible points, particularly the port of Rashin, could escape observation, though informed foreign opinion discounted the rumors.

subfiles.title: Dairen Telegram No. 9 on Troops Entraining North
subfiles.about: Reports that landings had slackened and many newly arrived troops were moving north by train.
subfiles.summary: After two more days of heavy debarkations, troop arrivals at Dairen diminished appreciably. Dairen, nearby areas, and probably Port Arthur remained crowded with infantry and remount cavalry, but many units stayed only briefly before entraining north. A train of at least fifty horse-drawn light wagons, thought to be ammunition carriers, was observed entering the railway station.

subfiles.title: Kobe Telegram on Three Weeks of Westbound Transport Departures
subfiles.about: Estimates that 300 transports had departed Kobe westbound during the previous three weeks.
subfiles.summary: Warner estimated that about 300 transports had left Kobe heading west during a three-week period. Departures on August 10 were especially numerous, and most vessels were lightly loaded, suggesting that they might be carrying troops rather than cargo.

subfiles.title: State Department Paraphrase for OPNAV of the Kobe Transport Report
subfiles.about: Forwards the Kobe report concerning large numbers of lightly loaded westbound transports.
subfiles.summary: The State Department retransmitted Warner's August 11 message to naval authorities. It emphasized the numerous lightly loaded vessels leaving on August 10 and the estimate of 300 westbound departures during the prior three weeks.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Shanghai Report on Japanese Troop Departures
subfiles.about: Reports continuing troop departures from Shanghai and preparations to withdraw most Japanese forces from Foochow.
subfiles.summary: Several thousand troops were reportedly leaving Shanghai each week, with the equivalent of two divisions departing since July 20, chiefly toward the south. The lack of heavy equipment suggested that complete divisions were not moving as units. Foreign sources also believed preparations were under way to evacuate most Japanese forces from Foochow, leaving only the detachment on the island at the Min River's mouth.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Japanese Military Personnel in Cochinchina
subfiles.about: References a report that only Colonel Saito and civilian assistants remained after Japanese naval and air departures from Saigon.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Saigon telegram No. 43 concerning Japanese military personnel in Cochinchina. Following the departure of the destroyer Isokaze and a Japanese bomber on April 4, only Colonel Saito and civilian assistants reportedly remained.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Report on Troops Sailing from Woosung
subfiles.about: Reports that roughly 24,000 troops sailed from Woosung with equipment and numerous landing boats.
subfiles.summary: Approximately 24,000 troops reportedly sailed from Woosung between November 15 and 23 with a large quantity of military equipment. The force carried at least 184 landing boats, indicating preparation for landings where normal port facilities were unavailable. Trucks moving out were newly camouflaged in green, and no comparably large coastal movements had yet been observed elsewhere.

subfiles.title: War Department Paraphrase on Japanese Officers Leaving the Panama Canal Zone
subfiles.to: War Department Intelligence Branch and other military recipients
subfiles.about: Reports the travel of three Japanese army officers from France Field to Bolivia and Peru en route to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Japanese army officers Rinkichi Kaneko, Eitoro Yusicka, and Atsunari Uchida left France Field after arriving from Mexico City. Yusicka proceeded to La Paz, while the other two traveled to Lima; all carried diplomatic passports and expected eventually to return to Tokyo. A G-2 comment linked their movements to press reports of a possible exodus of Japanese officials from Mexico amid fears of war with the United States.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Chinese Ambassador Wei Tao-ming
subfiles.about: Records the Chinese ambassador's assessment of Japanese manpower, shipping, and unexplained troop movements.
subfiles.summary: Wei Tao-ming called to present his credentials and discussed Japan's prospective weaknesses in manpower and shipping. He could not explain large troop movements away from strategic air bases in China or determine their direction, but believed they indicated an important development. He added that wireless stations along the Chinese coast, through Indochina, and into Burma were unusually active.
